It's Black Friday week and the Apple discounts keep on coming! If you're after a new MacBook, Apple Watch, iPad, or a different piece of Apple gear, then now is the best time to buy, as we're seeing some absolutely killer deals.
Take the always-in-demand MacBook Neo, which has received one of its first major discounts since the price rose to $699 earlier in the year. It's currently available for just $649 at Amazon. If you need a machine with a little more power, then there are also big savings to be had on various MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models.
Deals don't stick around forever, and some are selling out quickly, so act fast if you see something that you like here.
We'll be on hand all day today, November 25, to bring you the best Apple deals we can find, so keep checking back to see what's new.
iPhone 18 Pro: free w/ new line + unlimited @ T-Mobile T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro for free when you open a new line and use three T-Mobile Picks. (T-Mobile's new data plans offer up to 3 Picks or free perks, such as DashPass by DoorDash or Netflix Standard. The number of Picks you get is based on the plan's price or how many phone lines are on your plan). In our iPhone 18 Pro review , we said it's the best phone money can buy. The iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.3-inch OLED 120Hz display (2622 x 1206), A20 Pro chipset, and 256GB of storage. You also get a 48MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP telephoto lens w/ 4x zoom, and an 18MP front camera.
In our AirPods Pro 3 review, we said these earbuds are the best AirPods yet. With features like Live Translation, heart rate tracking, and integrated Siri, they're ideal if you want your earbuds to work for you. But if you "just" want industry-leading earbuds with perfect sound and great ANC, the Pro 3 won't let you down.
Price check: $149 @ Walmart | Sold out @ Amazon
Apple Watch Series 12 delivers the line's most accurate heart rate sensing yet, alongside a suite of advanced health and fitness features. It's powered by Apple's new S11 chip, which enables new Audio Intelligence features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap.
I didn't expect to see this deal. The new iPad mini A20 Pro is $100 off. The new model sports a larger 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR Display (2316 x 1512), A20 Pro CPU, 24% smaller bezels than its predecessor, and better audio. You also get a 12MP camera on the front and back and Wi-Fi 7 support. The base models (128GB/256GB) boast a 5-core CPU with 2 super cores and 3 efficiency cores, whereas the 512GB model bumps it to a 6-core CPU with 2 super cores and 4 efficiency cores. This is the first time it's on sale.
The Mac mini M6 keeps the ultra-compact 5x5-inch design introduced with the prior generation, but packs major performance upgrades under the hood. You get the raw speed of Apple's M6 chip, upgraded graphics with hardware-accelerated ray tracing for better 1080p gaming, 16GB of unified memory, and improved connectivity thanks to Apple's custom N1 chip, which adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread support.
Let's kick the day off with a tasty iPad deal! Amazon is cutting $100 off the retail price of a couple of iPad minis.
If you're on a tight budget then why not try the iPad mini 7? Sure, it's a slightly older model, but it means you can get a great tablet for less than $500 at Amazon.
If you have a little more money to play with then the iPad mini 8 is also available and now down to $599. For that extra $100 you get an OLED display which will really make your movies and photos sparkle.
This week we've noticed the AirPods Pro 3 have dropped to a record-low price of $149 over at Amazon. There's no telling how long this offer will last so it's worth snapping up the second you read this. These are some of the best earbuds money can buy and a no-brainer if you're already committed to the Apple ecosystem. Heck, at this price — I'd buy two pairs and gift one to a family member.
Not everyone needs to go Ultra, and the Apple Watch Series 12 is pretty much the "Goldilocks" smartwatch that'll track your health and fitness, let you respond to notifications and not look out of place when paired with smart dress on a night out.
I'm currently on an Apple Watch Series 10 and eyeing up this deal on the Series 12. Apple has upped its game when it comes to wellness, introducing a daily readiness score this year following the sleep score that it introduced last year. This gives you a great snapshot into your health, and if you want to dig deeper, you can.
$100 off the current-gen Apple Watch is a deal I would expect to see over the course of this week, but I'd snag this one ASAP before all the colors sell out.
Here's a very good deal for anyone looking to pick up the latest MacBook Pro. Right now, Amazon has knocked $200 off the new 14-inch MacBook Pro M6. And you can knock a further $20 off that with the coupon.
Our review of the MacBook Pro 14-inch M6 notes its a modest update, but there's still a ton of performance under the aluminum hood and the 14-inch display is as sharp as ever. Due to all the price hikes this year, the M6 is $400 more than the previous model. That's not great, but this discount takes some of the sting out of it. If you're on the hunt for a new MacBook, this is the week you're going to want to pull the trigger.
I have AirTags for everything. I have them on two different sets of keys, in my backpack, attached to my bike and, of course, one stashed safely away in my wallet. And I've never paid full price for any of them.
Right now, you can grab four AirTags for $79, down from the usual price of $99. That works out at under $20 per AirTag. This is a deal that comes round most years on retail events like Black Friday and it's always worth taking advantage of.
I don't have personal experience with the AirPods Max 2... but I've used their predecessor for years and can vouch for the quality of Apple's over-ears efforts. My colleague Erin reviewed the AirPods Max 2 back in March and praised the bright, energetic mids and melodic, controlled bass.
The design hasn't changed from the first generation, so while they are a bit on the heavy side, the AirPods Max 2 spread the weight nicely with the mesh headband. As with the AirPods Pro 3, the real benefit of these is Apple's multi-pairing. You can go from listening to music on your iPhone to watching a video on your iPad in a heartbeat. I've never been crazy about the price, but then this Black Friday deal is a big step back in the right direction.
RAMageddon may have driven up the price of one of our favorite laptops, but the MacBook Neo just got a nice discount for Black Friday!
The specs sound a bit bizarre on paper – an a18 Pro out of an iPhone and 8GB of RAM. But as it turns out, macOS is so well optimized that this is all you need for a sleek, zippy experience.
This is an ideal productivity machine for students and those on a budget who don’t want to give up those premium niceties like an aluminium design.
I'm not going to lie: I'd like to see a larger discount than just $50 on the A16 iPad 11-inch. But at the same time, if I was going to recommend and iPad to most people, it would be this one. You get a bright Liquid Retina display, a 10-hour battery life, and you can accessorize it with the Apple Folio keyboard or Apple Pencil.
If you just want a tablet for a bit of light productivity alongside listening alongside your regular media consumption, then there's no reason not to pick this one. Especially as you can pocket $50 with this Best Buy deal.
Unfortunately, I can't tell you that Verizon has knocked a ton of money off the excellent iPhone 18 Pro for Black Friday. But, if you sign up for a three-year Simplicity Plus or Simplicity Pro plan

articles.title_zh:
DW News. . China, the EU, Japan and India could face new US tariffs under a proposal targeting what the Trump administration calls overproduction. The measure would impose tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 major economies, with officials arguing that excess production abroad is hurting American manufacturers. The move comes after courts struck down some of Trump's earlier tariffs.

#DWBusiness
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

articles.title_orig: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
articles.title_zh: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
articles.content_orig:
Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 people
Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished
The tanker crossed the highway's central reservation before overturning and bursting into flames, local media report
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin proposes new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump admin proposes new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and some European Union countries, marking the latest escalation in global trade tensions.
"We're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on CNBC Wednesday morning.
President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his economic policy, but has suffered significant defeats in court -- including the Supreme Court's move earlier this year to invalidate most of the global tariffs his administration imposed. Tariffs were also a key issue in the midterm elections, during which Republicans suffered major losses as Democrats took back control of both chambers of Congress.
The administration says the new levies would be enforced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, where the U.S. is permitted to respond accordingly if it determines that other countries are participating in unfair trade practices that harm the U.S.
The USTR conducted a series of investigations into countries’ trade practices, announcing on Wednesday that they have determined "the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce." The USTR said its investigations into Norway and Mexico are ongoing.
These proposed tariffs will replace Trump's other levies that the Supreme Court invalidated in their ruling.
A senior administration official clarified that these tariffs are not "blanket" tariffs and that they are "targeted" to each specific country. They are also not expected to stack on top of existing duties, except for China.
The administration is proposing an additional 20% tariff on China, but threatened to double it to 40% if China does not abide by the agreed-upon trade truce as talks continue, according to a senior administration official. The new tariffs would be added on top of preexisting 25% forced tech transfer tariffs.
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun reacted to the news of the proposed tariffs in a press conference on Wednesday.
"Our position on handling China-U.S. economic and trade issues is consistent and clear. Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests. Relevant issues should be resolved through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit," Jiakun said.
This comes just a week after Trump visited China for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
China is among the several countries that have objected to tariffs under the Trump administration. A senior administration official said all of the countries have been informed of these new proposed tariffs, including China, and added that they do not expect retaliatory action.
There is no immediate impact of this announcement as a public comment period would be required to first take place, with the administration eyeing January as the earliest target date to fulfill such requirements.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now," Greer said on CNBC.
Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden said in a statement that the proposed tariffs are "not the solution."
"Only weeks after Americans overwhelmingly voted against his high tariffs and higher prices agenda, he’s back with another round. This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses," Wyden, a Democrat, said.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, blasted the proposed tariffs.
"The bad actor here is China, and instead of addressing the problem, Trump continues to let them dictate the terms while alienating our allies and passing the costs onto American families, with little benefit for American workers," he wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.
Separately, the U.S. is also considering modifying Brazil tariffs by increasing taxes on sugar and aircraft products.
"Today’s proposed modification would provide greater leverage to obtain the elimination of Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices," Greer said in a statement on Wednesday.
Greer's statement argued that imposing an "additional, specific tariff” on Brazil sugar imports as well as a 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports “is intended to help bring Brazil to the table" over what the U.S. perceives to be trade practice violations.
That action also would not be immediate, as the USTR says it will hold a hearing about Brazil's proposed tariff changes on Jan. 14.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push for Nvidia’s Huang appears to sideline China-hawks
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push for Nvidia’s Huang appears to sideline China-hawks
articles.content_orig:
President Trump made it clear to advisers on Friday: He wanted Jensen Huang back at Nvidia .
It had been less than two weeks since the computing giant's CEO and founder had resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose firm had allegedly funneled Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia's share price spiraled, imperiling a company whose semiconductors and financing deals have helped power the U.S. artificial intelligence boom.
The president had been on the phone with various Wall Street and Silicon Valley titans. The main takeaway from those conversations: The U.S. needs a strong Nvidia.
Mr. Trump was also privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.
Nvidia's board chair told investors on Tuesday of last week that the company did not intend to reinstate Huang. But before the end of the week, the board was privately signaling to the White House that it was serious about bringing him back. Board members just wanted to examine it from all angles first.
Huang's surprise comeback as CEO on Monday came after Trump and his team spent the weekend working on making it happen, in part by offering the Nvidia board a range of legal assurances about Huang. After the deal was done and the tech giant's shares surged, Mr. Trump publicly celebrated it, telling CNBC that he "convinced them" to rehire him.
CBS News spoke with U.S. officials and others directly familiar with the negotiations about how the deal came together.
Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel. Huang privately shared with the White House that he felt the board wanted to bring him back, but would need to be assured that the U.S. government didn't think he was a national security risk.
In phone calls, board members were told Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation, that the government had no legal issues with him, and that the administration wouldn't view his return to Nvidia's helm as a problem.
But what about Alice Huang, they wanted to know. She's the woman with whom Huang had an affair, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed. The White House made it clear their assurances didn't extend to her.
Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. The company was put on a U.S. trade blacklist this week, and it has been investigated by the Justice and Commerce departments.
Trump, Vance and board members hashed over the next steps. The board wanted to know what Mr. Trump would say publicly. They wanted Attorney General Todd Blanche himself to confirm Huang wasn't under investigation. The attorney general was comfortable with this.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton had conducted a deep dive into U.S. intelligence related to Alice Huang and her interactions with Jensen Huang. The information was circulated to Trump and senior officials.
Mr. Trump later told CNBC that Huang was "exonerated" after a "pretty good investigation."
Clayton, who previously led the Securities and Exchange Commission, helped connect Nvidia board members to administration officials for backdoor discussions, according to the sources, though he was not involved in the discussions surrounding Huang's reinstatement this weekend.
Clayton was also consulted by the president and others in the administration for his expertise in corporate governance matters.
On Sunday, Jensen Huang met with the board for hours.
Afterward, board members called the White House.
Earlier, Mr. Trump had discussed the prospect of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, though Lutnick was not involved in the weekend strategizing.
Lutnick's Commerce Department is responsible for enforcing export controls on advanced semiconductor chips — and since the Nvidia scandal erupted, he has been accused of not doing enough to prevent their diversion to China.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent openly suggested the Commerce Department had failed to act, saying other government agencies had supported putting Alice Huang's company Megaspeed on a trade blacklist "for months," but "Commerce has the pen."
Billionaire Elon Musk spoke with Mr. Trump about export controls and told Trump officials that the people he knew in the tech and business communities were steadfastly behind Huang.
Two senior national security officials were not involved in the effort to reinstate Huang: CIA director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio.
Earlier this year, Rubio had prepared a classified memorandum, based on U.S. intelligence that included intercepts of Alice Huang's conversations, warning Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was known to be in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security.
Rubio also briefed Mr. Trump on the intelligence aboard Air Force One in May, before Jensen Huang joined the presidential delegation en route to China during a stop in Alaska.
Allies of both Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS News on Monday that both men had expressed private concern about aspects of Huang's return but have so far not weighed breaking with Mr. Trump publicly over it. Some of their supporters, the sources said, have voiced their alarm about Rubio and Bessent standing by Mr. Trump on this decision.
Rubio was particularly angry when the news of Huang's reinstatement broke on Monday morning.
On Sunday, as Vance continued to press the Nvidia board, Bessent was asked in an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan " about his previous comment that Nvidia's board should go "outside" to find new leadership. He responded, "Well, Jensen is on the outside now."
Late Sunday night, the board shared with Mr. Trump and the vice president that Nvidia would announce before the markets opened Monday that Jensen Huang was being reinstated as president, CEO and board director.
"We were told, 'This is going to happen,'" one official told CBS News.
The language the two sides had gone over — that Mr. Trump's post on Truth Social would hail the decision and say Nvidia should cooperate with continued probes into Megaspeed and chip exports — was finalized. The White House told board members they could reveal publicly that they had been given assurances by the U.S. government that Jensen Huang did not pose a national security risk.
Nvidia is likely to continue to draw scrutiny as the FBI and Justice Department's National Security Division examine potential export control violations involving Megaspeed and another company, Super Micro Computer.
Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns about Jensen Huang's return. He is scheduled to appear before House and Senate panels next week.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq, S&P 500 end down, but well off lows as investors buy bargains
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq, S&P 500 end down, but well off lows as investors buy bargains
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points lower at 4.866%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 2 basis points at 4.65%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 3 basis points lower at 5.254%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate.
The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December.
"[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire."
Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday , with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction.
Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.title_zh: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia . Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.
Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC , the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.
But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill , who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."
Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections , as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.
"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."
Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.
"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.
"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.
Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.
There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."
"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.
Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.
"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin , D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.
"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"
Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.
At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.
"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.
Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.
"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security,"  MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."
Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."
Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk , who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."
But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.
"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.
"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

articles.title_orig: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.title_zh: Russia has passed the biggest military budget since Soviet times
articles.content_orig:
Russia’s State Duma has passed the third reading of a federal budget bill for 2027–2029 that allocates over 50 trillion rubles (approximately $609 billion) to defense, according to the Russian parliament’s official television channel, Duma TV , as reported by Militarnyi .
Under the State Duma Defense Committee’s conclusion on draft law No. 615-9, Russia plans to spend 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion) on defense in 2027, marking an increase of roughly one-third compared to the 12.93 trillion rubles ($157.4 billion) allocated for 2026 in the previous budget plan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the next three years, total funding for national defense will reach 50.05 trillion rubles ($609.3 billion). Specifically, Moscow plans to allocate 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.8 billion, or 6.91% of GDP) in 2027, 16.61 trillion rubles ($202.2 billion, or 6.3% of GDP) in 2028, and 16.30 trillion rubles ($198.4 billion, or 5.79% of GDP) in 2029. These figures include both public and classified budget expenditures under the “National Defense” category.
Compared to the previous three-year budget plan, defense funding has been increased by 3.58 trillion rubles ($43.6 billion) for 2027 and by 3.56 trillion rubles ($43.3 billion) for 2028.
Overall, total spending for Russia’s federal budget in 2027 is set at 48.74 trillion rubles ($593.3 billion). Direct spending on national defense will account for roughly 35.2% of all federal expenditures, not including additional funding for security and law enforcement agencies listed under other budget sections.
In total, national defense spending in the 2027–2029 budget exceeds the previous three-year budget plan by approximately 10.5 trillion rubles ($127.8 billion).
According to The Moscow Times , this surge in military expenditures will be accompanied by funding cuts across several civilian sectors. Compared to the 2026 figures outlined in the prior budget plan, spending on the national economy will drop by roughly 3%, housing and communal services by 8%, healthcare by 3%, and social policy by 6%.
Russia’s federal budget deficit for 2027 is projected at 5.44 trillion rubles ($66.2 billion), or 2.2% of GDP, with government borrowing expected to serve as the primary source for covering the shortfall.
Previously, it was reported that Russia’s Central Bank has been selling gold from its reserves for ten consecutive months to help cover a widening federal budget deficit, projected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, twice the amount initially anticipated.
The latest reduction brought the country’s total gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019.
The State Duma is the lower house of Russia's parliament, the Federal Assembly, responsible for drafting and passing federal laws along with approving certain government appointments.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Slump Again as Investors Fret About A.I., Tariffs and Inflation
articles.title_zh: Stocks Slump Again as Investors Fret About A.I., Tariffs and Inflation
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading.
But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day.
An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000.
Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes.  After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day.
The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry.
But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high.
Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period.
AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Swoon as AI Fears Spur Rush to Treasuries: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Swoon as AI Fears Spur Rush to Treasuries: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.
The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.
The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.
But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.
"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.
Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Dow closes higher Wednesday, wiping out 1,100-point loss in stunning rebound: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow closes higher Wednesday, wiping out 1,100-point loss in stunning rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday as Wall Street tried to recover from steep declines led by artificial intelligence-linked stocks.
The blue-chip Dow advanced 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
Stocks came well off their lows as the session went on. The blue-chip Dow lost more than 1,100 points, or 2.2% at its low of the day. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 4.6%, and the broad market S&P 500 shed 3.2% at their respective lows.
Traders chalked up part of the rebound to light trading ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday as well as the circulation of a blog post by Michael Burry, in which he said that his portfolio is " temporarily almost entirely long ."
The Dow was boosted by gains in stocks such as International Business Machines , Salesforce and Sherwin-Williams . S&P 500 sectors such as materials, energy and real estate were all higher, bolstering the index.
However, Nvidia led AI-related stocks lower, dropping almost 4%. Micron Technology moved down 4.5%, while Oracle declined more than 5%, and Alphabet shed more than 2%. The State Street Technology Select Sector ETF (XLK) ended nearly 1% lower.
Meanwhile, semiconductor stock Ambarella plummeted more than 19% after its forecast for the current quarter came in light . The company's earnings and revenue for the third quarter also missed expectations.
"This market is very bifurcated" between AI and non-AI stocks, said David Wagner, head of equities at Aptus Capital Advisors. "The market is pulling back obviously due to a pullback in tech, pullback in semis, pullback in the AI narrative, but right now, I don't see that being a growth scare. I see it being a sentiment-based scare" based on factors such as the composition of Congress in the new year, he added.
To be sure, there's still a "big worry" among investors that the worries in AI could move from a sentiment-based scare to a growth-based scare "if the market starts pricing in too much Fed activity of hiking rates," Wagner also said.
October's personal consumption expenditures price index reading showed that inflation still isn't slowing down, which reiterated expectations for interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve in December and January and put investors in a risk-off mood.
Headline PCE rose 0.3% last month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.8%. While both figures were in line with expectations, the annual rate increased from 3.7% in September. Excluding food and energy prices, core PCE increased 3.3% year over year, coming in slightly above the Dow Jones forecast.
Investor sentiment was also weighed by the White House unveiling a barrage of new tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
Wall Street is coming off a losing session for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, after tech stocks gave back some of their gains from the prior session as Nvidia sank and Anthropic fell below its IPO price.
Tuesday's choppy trading action was just the latest in a volatile month. Even before the ouster and reinstatement of Nvidia's Jensen Huang — which sent stocks soaring Monday — and Democrats' sweep in the midterm elections, investors were deliberating the future of the artificial intelligence build-out amid a worsening macroeconomic outlook.
The U.S. stock market will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving. The market will also close at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended the session in positive territory.
The 30-stock Dow added 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to 50,182.95. On the flip side, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell 0.25% and 0.62% to 7,182.78 and 23,585.80, respectively.
The stock market has sharply curtailed its losses, with the S&P 500 now down about 0.3% versus its slump of 3.2% earlier Wednesday.
The stocks that have seen the biggest bounce from their session lows Coherent , Axon Enterprise and Bloom Energy . See below for a few of the names that have also rebounded.
— Darla Mercado and Nick Wells
U.S. consumers plan to spend more this holiday season, with higher-income households driving the increase while lower-income shoppers pulling back, according to a recent Citi survey.
The survey of about 2,500 consumers conducted with Citi's Innovation Lab from Nov. 5 to Nov. 16 showed  that respondents plan to spend 12% more than 2025 holiday season, highlighting the K-shaped consumer theme.
Inflation remained a concern, with 72% of respondents at least somewhat worried about food and fuel prices. Among those cutting spending, 48% said higher food and fuel costs, up from 39% last year. Shoppers reported price increases across all 11 categories surveyed, led by groceries, clothing, electronics, and home improvement.
Higher-income households are driving the gain with households earning more than $100k planning to spend $1,202, up 34%, while those earning under $25,000 expect to spend $295, down 3%.
The divide reflects a reversal from last year, when the highest-income group planned the steepest spending cut (-15%) and the lowest-income group was the only one expecting to spend more (+6%), Citi wrote.
SpaceX has received authorization from the Federal Communications Commission to launch 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites into orbit, leading its shares to rise.
The company's chairman Brendan Carr said Wednesday in an social media post that the approval would help "extend America's lead in Super Intelligence."
Shares of the space company ticked up more than 1% on Wednesday.
Ratings agency S&P Global put Nvidia 's rating on "CreditWatch Negative," pointing to rising risks from the company's management and governance framework.
Nvidia currently has an issuer credit rating of AA.
"Recent well-publicized developments have raised questions about the effectiveness of NVIDIA Corp.'s management and governance framework, including board independence and 'key man' risk," the ratings agency said in a Wednesday announcement .
The artificial intelligence bellwether has been making headlines – and has seen its stock make sharp swings – following the controversial exit and reinstatement of its CEO Jensen Huang. In November alone, shares are down 27%.
" News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in NVIDIA's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," the rating agency said.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) was down more than 2% on Wednesday, adding to its recent losses and pacing for its worst performance over 10 trading sessions in more than a year.
The fund — which shed 7.3% on Tuesday — has fallen more than 17% since the Nov. 11 close. If that holds through Wednesday's close, the fund will record its worst 10-day period since April 2025.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
Michael Burry is "almost entirely long" on stocks, even as various areas of the market continue to sell off, the investor said Wednesday in a recent edition of his newsletter.
"Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," Burry wrote in the Substack post. "In fact, when I say less short, right now apart from Palantir puts and MetLife puts, I am temporarily almost entirely long. Temporarily, because I am continuing to assess short opportunities."
Gold futures bounced a bit off sessions lows today after touching a low of $3,425.2 per troy ounce, a move that marked the first time below 3,500 since the end of August 2025.
Futures were last trading down 1.5% at $3,508.90.
Gold has fallen about 10% this month, pacing for its third straight monthly decline. Including November, gold has had three double-digit monthly declines this year.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
The three major averages trimmed losses in midday trading Wednesday, coming back from session lows.

articles.title_orig: Chinese intel may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO, U.S. agencies tell Congress
articles.title_zh: Chinese intel may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO, U.S. agencies tell Congress
articles.content_orig:
China's Ministry of State Security may have been surveilling Alice Huang and sought information from her after her affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began, U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers Tuesday, according to people familiar with the briefing.
While there are still gaps in what U.S. intelligence agencies know, there is no indication to date that Alice Huang was specifically tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or that she passed information of significant value to the Chinese intelligence service.
But she was known to U.S. intelligence agencies to have been in contact with an MSS officer starting at least in spring 2025, multiple sources said, and her contacts with the agency raised counterintelligence concerns among U.S. intelligence officials. China's intelligence services rely not only on trained officers and formally recruited assets but also on citizens who are obliged under Chinese law to provide assistance when called upon.
Congressional staffers were also told that Kang Wei, believed to be Alice Huang's husband, had more extensive ties to the MSS, people familiar with the briefing said.
The New York Times was first to report on the briefing.
The two-hour briefing for House and Senate Intelligence Committee staffers, which included senior analysts from across the U.S. intelligence community, came two days after President Trump intervened to secure Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, despite national security concerns raised by some of his senior advisers.
Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under U.S. investigation for potentially diverting sensitive American technology to China.
Concerns about Alice Huang were laid out in a classified memo drafted this spring by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio that summarized U.S. intelligence, including intercepted communications involving the former Megaspeed executive. It was intended to ensure senior administration officials involved in relevant policy decisions were aware of the potential counterintelligence risks posed by her interactions with Jensen Huang.
Among those who received the memo were Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and senior White House staff. Rubio also briefed the president on intelligence.
The memo was not provided during Tuesday's briefing, despite requests from both congressional intelligence committees to see it.
China has denied allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.
Shortly after the existence of the memo came to light earlier this month, Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an extramarital affair. He later resigned as Nvidia CEO, but after less than two weeks, the company's board of directors reinstated him.
The reinstatement came after Trump administration officials offered Nvidia assurances that Jensen Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation and that the government had no legal issues with him, CBS News reported earlier Wednesday . The assurances did not extend to Alice Huang.
Two criminal investigations involving potential violations of U.S. export controls by Megaspeed and another buyer of Nvidia chips, Super Micro Computer, remain ongoing. The FBI has been investigating both cases for more than a year, with the Justice Department's National Security Division leading the Megaspeed investigation. Megaspeed has denied any violations of U.S. export control laws and says Alice Huang left the company last year.
Jensen Huang is expected on Capitol Hill next week for a closed-door session with House lawmakers and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee.

SpaceX ( SPCX ) said Wednesday it will give one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk personally matching the company's contribution.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement . "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
SpaceX also said president and COO Gwynne Shotwell had separately announced a personal gift of more than 2 million shares.
Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for children, created under the president's 2025 tax law. The program officially launched in July, with the government providing a one-time $1,000 contribution for eligible children born from 2025 through 2028.
Last month, the White House said nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through automatic enrollment.
Since the July 4 launch, more than $4.5 billion has been deposited, including $1.3 billion in $1,000 government seed contributions, according to the White House.
Other public companies have also pledged funds to the accounts. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a CNBC interview last week that an Anthropic ( ANT ) co-founder will make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts in the coming weeks.
"We believe that it's important for these great entrepreneurs to share their bounty," he added.

articles.title_orig: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
articles.title_zh: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
articles.content_orig:
Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.
Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.
According to the company, Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers. Compared to the number of people using Google Search or even Bing or DuckDuckGo, that’s not much. But the pitch is that with Google, the user is the product, not the customer, and that paying anywhere from $5 to $25 per month (there are multiple plans; unlimited search queries is in the $10 per month plan) helps users escape from that devil’s bargain.
Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.
The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)
Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.
Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Receives Government Approval to Launch Space Data Centers
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Receives Government Approval to Launch Space Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.
