articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Keeps Falling. It’s Obvious Jensen Was Not the Only Problem.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Keeps Falling. It’s Obvious Jensen Was Not the Only Problem.
articles.content_orig:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 46% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by about $2.6 trillion. The stock is now trading at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet .
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

articles.title_orig: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday accused Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang of violating federal laws limiting advanced technology exports to China .
In a post on X, Schumer said Huang "shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race."
Nvidia and the White House did not immediately comment.
Schumer's statement marked an escalation of congressional criticism against Huang, who was reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday despite claims regarding his relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese government agent. Lawmakers from both parties are increasingly questioning Nvidia's trade with China, pressing for tighter controls while investigating whether Huang's conduct endangered national security.
Lawmakers have also faulted President Donald Trump for pushing Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.
Schumer and other legislators insist Congress must act rapidly to curtail American chip sales to China. Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said: "Congress must get to the bottom of what happened, and then strengthen our export controls to ensure China can't access our most advanced chips through the back door."
In a separate move on Tuesday, leading Democrats on four House committees wrote to Trump demanding answers about his awareness of Huang’s ties to the suspected agent.
"Your personal relationship with Mr. Huang and your willful blindness to the economic and national security risks posed by this scandal have put the American people at great risk," wrote Representatives Frank Pallone, Gregory Meeks, Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia, requesting all records of administration contact with the Nvidia board.
"Upon learning that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected agent of the Chinese government, what actions, if any, did Trump take to limit risks to America’s economic and national security?" the lawmakers inquired.
Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, told CNBC on Tuesday that more protections are needed on exports to China. "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang," he stated, adding it would be "just to make sure that he doesn't do something that is going to risk the United States."
Huang will appear on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing, panel's chair Tim Scott announced Monday.
Huang is also slated for a private briefing on December 1 with three House panels.
Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, said Huang's "reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake." He noted: "We sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law. That is a dangerous precedent to set."

articles.title_orig: Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)
articles.title_zh: Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)
articles.content_orig:
A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.
"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.
Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.
Heather Kutryk said her family had been preparing for years prior to her husband's mission, calling it "a long time coming"
Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.
The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".
Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".
"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.
"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."
In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

articles.title_orig: Why this stock-market selloff is probably going to get worse before it gets better
articles.title_zh: Why this stock-market selloff is probably going to get worse before it gets better
articles.content_orig:
By The Premium Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:51AM EST
Investors have had a wild few days. On Friday, all three major U.S. indexes closed in correction territory, at least 10% below their recent highs. On Monday, the S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%, both their best days since April 2025. The rally came after the board of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.91% ) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%, its eighth loss in nine sessions, and the Nasdaq fell 1.48%. This morning, S&P 500 futures were down around 1% in pre-market trading, and Nasdaq-100 futures were down 1.61%.
So, have we seen the bottom?
Over the weekend, Motley Fool CEO and co-founder Tom Gardner pulled together a free, live Markets Special Report at short notice to help investors make sense of the sell-off. He was joined by TMF's chief investment officer Andy Cross and analysts from Team Hidden Gems and Team Rule Breakers. During Sunday evening's livestream, a member put that very question to the panel. The market will probably fall further at some point, Andy said. He just didn't know whether that would happen this year.
Team Rule Breakers' Jason Hall turned the question around. He asked members whether they had "structured your financial life so that this is a fun academic exercise." If you're living and dying by whether this is the bottom, he said, something else in your investing plan may need fixing.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Just look at Nvidia. On Sunday night, Huang was out as CEO, and the panel debated whether to buy more shares. Team Hidden Gems' Matt Frankel said the board should at least consider bringing him back. The next morning, it did, and the stock closed up 31%.
Big swings are normal. Andy pointed out that the market has historically fallen about 10% roughly once a year, 15% about every two years and 20% about every five years. It has also risen in about three years out of four.
As one member reminded the panel, quoting investor Peter Lynch, nobody rings a bell at the top or the bottom. So Tom suggests buying in a U shape. Don't try to pick the exact low. Keep adding a little at a time as prices fall and then recover.
A better question is whether your portfolio can cope with whatever comes next. Our investing principles can help.
None of this means the market can't fall further, or for longer. Tom pointed to Japan, where investors who bought at the 1989 peak were still sitting on losses more than 25 years later.
So what would worry the panel more? Matt would be concerned if company earnings slowed sharply. Andy pointed to inflation that won't go away. Jose said he'd watch for AI companies cutting back on data center spending. And Tom flagged signs that sales are getting weaker, such as customers taking longer to pay their bills. We'll be watching all four.
Potential Growth Indicator (PGI): Our PGI compares the cash sitting on the sidelines with the stock market's total value. It stood at 11.47% at the time of writing on Wednesday morning, up from 10.83% on Sunday. That puts it just above its long-run norm of about 11%. Historically, readings above 13% have been good times to buy. Readings near 10% or below point to more speculation.
VIX: The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, uses options prices to measure how much the S&P 500 is expected to swing over the next 30 days. It tends to jump when stocks fall. That's why it's often called Wall Street's "fear gauge." It was around 35 after Friday's sell-off. Tom noted that readings above 35 have often been attractive times to add to stocks. By Tuesday's close, it had eased to about 26.
Beta: You'll find this on any stock's TMF ticker page. It shows how volatile a stock is compared with the S&P 500. A stock with a beta of 2 tends to move about twice as much as the market, so expect it to fall harder in a sell-off.
Nobody knows if Friday was the low. This week showed how fast things can change. But if you hold some cash, own a broad mix of stocks and think in five-year stretches, you don't need to know. As Jason put it, the bottom then becomes a fun academic exercise.
When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 785 %* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 200 % for the S&P 500.
They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor.

articles.title_orig: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.title_zh: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.content_orig:
If we learned one thing form the browser wars of the 2000s, it’s that having a single ecosystem dominate the internet is best avoided. Yet here we are in 2026, and through Google’s Blink and Apple’s Webkit, we have very little diversity in the world of web browsing engines. Firefox is now very much an outsider, and that’s pretty much it. But there is another up-and-coming fully-featured browser, Ladybird, and it’s now available in alpha form for those of you with macOS or Linux.
This browser had an unlikely start, as a component of the esoteric operating system, SerenityOS. We tested it in that form and found it competent, but the process of running the OS in a VM, not so much. It was split into a separate project in 2024, and since then they have been working towards this point, of having something close to a release version.
We’ve followed Ladybird for a while now, not because we expect the world to adopt it en masse, but because, incredibly, it’s now the third major in-development browser engine family. Just as we needed the Konqueror-derived Webkit a couple of decades ago to provide a balance to the then-dominant Internet Explorer, we may need this piece of software at some point. We’ll give it a try, and perhaps you will too.
If only it had extensions (for my password manager+some random things) and userstyles and userscripts.
This makes me think that a good next target for an AI assisted software liberation would probably be web browsers. Yes, Firefox is open source, but the official releases are all run by a group of opinionated people who do it for a living. That financial support requirement understandably makes people conservative about taking risks. A modern AI assisted fork of any open source browser could do great things.
What great things exactly? I keep hearing about these great things but never what they are. Will they be as great as the slop that are those supposedly incredible apps that will kill Adobe?
Also lol about taking risks. What risks do you want to take? Firefox lost users exactly because it was “taking risks” and making stupid decisions.
An AI assisted fork will die as soon as it is released because nobody would give a shit about it.
“What great things exactly? I keep hearing about these great things but never what they are…”
Cat memes. The answer is reallly, really good cat memes.  That’s the whole point of AI…. Well… That and the extinction of the human species.
That sounds like a recipe for disaster honestly.
Browsers are undoubtedly the second most important thing besides the operating system itself and is through which nearly ALL our personal data goes including authentication data. The potential for disastrous consequences if there is any malice or neglect involved is incredibly high.
Trust isn’t to be given lightly with most serious browser forks and implementations taking ages to build rapport and the aspect of that those working on it are doing it for a living actually gives points in its favor. Trusting some random one-off AI Agent made fork among a flood of thousands of such: Seems like a very bad idea.
Good thing, then, that this isn’t a new project, and has a history that you can refer to.

China launched an international astronaut, Pakistan's first space traveler to reach orbit, to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program.
A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25).
Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong space station , a three-module orbital lab that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022.
Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .)
China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training.
We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch.
This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest.
Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu.
Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 .
According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.content_orig:

US GDP growth in the third quarter was revised strongly upwards on Wednesday, with the Commerce Department citing strong investment and consumer spending, as the Fed's preferred inflation gauge hit a three-year high in October.
US GDP growth in the third quarter this year was estimated at 4.3 percent at an annualized rate, the department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said, a rise of 0.9 percentage points from the previous estimate and much higher than market expectations.
"Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports," the BEA said in a statement.
The US economy has shown resilient growth in recent months despite facing significant headwinds, including from President Donald Trump's chaotic tariff policies and his war on Iran, which has driven up energy prices.
Also on Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge came in at a three-year high in October, according to BEA data, with a rise in energy prices accompanied by an increase in nondurable goods inflation.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index rose by 3.8 percent year-on-year in October, the data showed, matching a three-year high set in May.
The US Federal Reserve has a long-term two-percent target for PCE inflation, one that it has missed for almost six years.
In September, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time in three years in order to combat the persistent price increases, which have battered US households and businesses.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held rates steady at its last meeting in October, but with inflation continuing to run hot, it is likely to raise rates at its next confab in December.
The years of above-target inflation since the pandemic have hit US households hard, with current price levels more than 30 percent higher than in 2020, as per the official Consumer Price Index.
Affordability was a key issue in this month's midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by their rival Democrats.
The price increases have been driven by Trump's tariffs, energy price increases due to the war on Iran and a massive investment boom in AI technology driving up demand for some goods.
Trump has defended his economic performance by pointing to data like GDP growth, which has been robust despite the headwinds, mainly on the back of the AI boom.
Economists warn that while consumer spending has remained strong, despite the high prices, there is a growing divide between lower- and higher-income households in the United States.
The Fed's latest "Beige Book," released Wednesday, said US consumers grappling with high consumer prices have been "increasingly selective" in discretionary purchases. Auto sales weakened in a move the report attributed to higher energy prices, while lofty lending rates were a drag on the housing market.
On the positive side, the report said employment levels "rose slightly," with contacts in several sectors citing "steady or rising labor demand."
Of the 12 districts across the country, eight reported "slight to moderate" growth while four reported no change, the Fed report said.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the fresh inflation data pointed to a likely rate hike in December, and possibly another a month later.
"America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," she said. "The Federal Reserve has to act in December and likely January."
She pointed out that while consumer spending did increase in absolute terms in October, it was flat once adjusted for inflation.
Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, said the strong GDP data would give Fed policymakers room to breathe when it comes to further rate hikes, which tend to cool economic activity as they tackle inflation.
"The tightening in financial market conditions, if sustained, will not have a noticeable impact on growth until the second half of next year," he said.

articles.title_orig: Russian Refinery Runs Drop to Lowest in Decades, Rystad Says
articles.title_zh: Russian Refinery Runs Drop to Lowest in Decades, Rystad Says
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has continued its attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said while threatening retaliation.
Putin made the threat on Tuesday, after Kyiv said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow did the same.
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for Saturday’s drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. One crew member was injured.
The Ukrainian leader told Bloomberg in an interview that the vessel, Sparta II, had been a legitimate target for his military as it was carrying weapons.
Ukrainian attacks on fuel installations subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire in the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But they picked up again in late October.
“We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.
“In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.”
He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.
According to estimates from two industry sources cited by the Reuters news agency, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October.
Several Russian regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of petrol and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.
Putin said that while the situation on the domestic fuel market remained difficult, petrol prices have stabilised after they peaked in October.
Elsewhere, Poland on Tuesday accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace when a Russian surveillance drone briefly crossed the border.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
Moscow on Monday accused Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state, of a range of hostile actions “on the verge of triggering open war”, after Estonia announced the closure of its land border.
In other incidents, Warsaw said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, and a Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in an attack claimed by Ukraine.
On Sunday, Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a Libyan port using maritime drones. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the drone attack was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli.
Additionally, British security officials on Tuesday warned United Kingdom companies providing “material support” for Ukrainian armed forces to brace for Russian sabotage attempts.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack killed two people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Tuesday.
Forty people, including four children, were wounded in the assault, Semikin added. Images and a video on his Telegram account showed a damaged apartment building with its windows blown out and rubble on the ground.
The Interfax news agency, citing Russia’s Defence Ministry, said on Tuesday that the Russian military hit drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine’s Sumy region, also killing a number of servicemen.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
articles.title_zh: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
articles.content_orig:
Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 2%.
"We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday.
"What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 5% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped about 2%, with some plunging further. Micron Technology declined 5%.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 4%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower.
AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft lost more than 1% and Meta traded higher.

articles.title_orig: FAA’s ‘line up and wait’ rule is in effect: How it could affect your flight
articles.title_zh: FAA’s ‘line up and wait’ rule is in effect: How it could affect your flight
articles.content_orig:
As millions of Americans prepare to fly for the Thanksgiving holiday, the Federal Aviation Administration is tightening the rules governing a common air traffic control practice used to keep flights moving.
Beginning Tuesday, controllers can only permit an aircraft to “Line Up and Wait” when their tower has a supervisor on duty who is not simultaneously working another control position.
The procedure allows controllers to move an aircraft on a runway before clearing it for takeoff, helping expedite departures.
Tracking US flight delays and cancellations in charts
It’s not clear why the FAA decided to implement the new rule during the busy Thanksgiving travel week. However the agency says the change “will not impact airport operations.”
Air traffic controllers have warned some pilots there could be backups.
“They are saying we need a standalone in-charge controller or supervisor behind us if we are to do it,” a controller in Albuquerque told a pilot on Monday, in audio recorded by ATC.com .
“That’s probably going to cause some delays,” the Southwest Airlines pilot responded.
“Yeah,” the controller agreed.
Nationally, the air traffic controllers’ union, NATCA, said their employees “will continue to perform their duties with the same professionalism, dedication, and commitment to safety that they demonstrate every day.”
To combat decades-long staffing problems, the FAA often combines air traffic controller responsibilities and often has someone both directing planes and supervising other controllers.
In the new directive issued by the FAA, the agency cited concerns about distractions when supervisors juggle multiple roles. The notice does not identify any specific safety incidents that prompted the change.

articles.title_orig: FAA Investigates Amazon Drone Crash in Michigan
articles.title_zh: FAA Investigates Amazon Drone Crash in Michigan
articles.content_orig:
A drone making a delivery for the online retailer Amazon crashed outside of Detroit on Friday after delivering a bottle of shampoo and now the Federal Aviation Administration is investigating.
The uncrewed vehicle successfully delivered the package to Jim Brennan’s Huntington Woods, Michigan, backyard shortly after his wife placed the order, he told CNN affiliate WXYZ .
“She ordered shampoo, and we just expected a truck to pull up, and then we get the notifications it’s coming by drone in seven minutes,” Brennan said.
The package was left in the backyard, but as he watched the Prime Air drone taking off, it hit a fiberoptic cable and knocked off a propeller.
“All of a sudden I realized it’s under a wire. It’s going to come up under that wire. And it did. And when it caught that, it just, it went crazy,” he said. “Like a sick bird, it tried to get out of here, but it couldn’t.”
Video recorded by Claire Brennan, who is not related to Jim Brennan, shows the aircraft struggling to fly before wobbling out of control and crashing as she walked by.
The drone landed on Logan Coomes’ garage next door, which he said had some minor damage.
“There’s a little corner on the tip of the peak of the garage where I think if it did rain, water would get through right now,” he told WXYZ. “Some shingles were flapped up from their original positions.”
No one was injured in the crash, Amazon said in a statement to CNN. The company removed the damaged drone from Coomes’ garage and is in contact with him.
“Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare,” Jack Stelzner, an Amazon spokesperson, said. “Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service.”
Prime Air drones have delivered hundreds of thousands of packages this year and nearly 6,000 are flown a day, Amazon said.
The “highly autonomous” MK30 drones can deliver items weighing five pounds or less, including groceries, cosmetics, medicine and electronics to the area surrounding their bases, the company said.
Locations are limited, but in August Amazon announced plans to reach nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of the year, a six-fold increase. The company plans to reach half a billion customers a year by the end of the decade.
The MK30 drones are designed to have a “best-in-class perception system to detect and avoid obstacles,” according to the company, and “navigate around obstacles like trampolines or clotheslines that may not have been captured in satellite imagery.”
Still, there have been crashes.
Last fall, Amazon ordered a brief halt to drone flights after two of its MK30 aircraft collided with a crane outside of Phoenix. No one was injured but the drones sustained substantial damage.
“We’ve completed our own internal review of this incident and are confident that there wasn’t an issue with the drones or the technology that supports them,” Terrence Clark, an Amazon spokesperson, told CNN at the time. “Nonetheless, we’ve introduced additional processes like enhanced visual landscape inspections to better monitor for moving obstructions such as cranes.”
CNN’s Alexandra Skores contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
articles.content_orig:
Democracy Defenders Fund spotlights systemic Trump family apparent conflicts of interest and policy remedies
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Democracy Defenders Fund’s new legal and ethics analysis addresses the reported conflicts arising from the Trump Revocable Trust’s Nvidia holdings and dozens of other Trump and family conflicts of interest. The report, The Family Legacy: Conflicts of Interest and Profiting from the Presidency , also includes detailed policy recommendations for Congress to claw back funds on behalf of the American people and to ban stock trades across all branches of government.
The Nvidia section of the analysis details how President Trump used his position to interfere in Nvidia’s affairs while maintaining personal investments in the company, calling the scandal and related severe national security and conflict of interest concerns a “profound ethics crisis.” The report spotlights the Nvidia stock trade history and timing of the transactions as critical factors in the president’s apparent conflicts of interest.
President Trump’s Revocable Trust contains a vast stock portfolio, including equity holdings in companies directly impacted by his administration’s decisions. Trump’s accounts have traded Nvidia stock over 100 times since he retook office, with transactions worth up to $97.5 million including selling $1 million in stock just days after receiving a briefing on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. President Trump is the Trump Revocable Trust’s sole beneficiary while his son, Donald Jr., serves as its trustee.
After Trump publicly pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang despite grave national security concerns regarding Huang’s ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, the company’s stock surged 33%, allowing Trump to personally pocket up to $15 million. The American public deserves to know whether Trump abused public office and manipulated markets to salvage the value of his own stock portfolio.
“President Trump used the power of his office to intervene in Nvidia’s affairs, brushing aside grave national security warnings and propping up the company’s stock value,” said Amb. Norm Eisen (ret.), co-founder and executive chair of Democracy Defenders Fund. “This is a corruption scandal unlike anything we’ve ever seen in American history, with the appearance of textbook market manipulation and possible insider trading coming straight from the Oval Office. Once again, we see that wealthy political allies are playing by a separate set of rules but no one, not even the president, is above the law. Congress must investigate and hold everyone involved in this accountable.”
This ongoing pattern of self-enrichment further underscores the troubling findings detailed in DDF’s report, which maps how the Trump family leverages the presidency for private financial gain. It includes a detailed analysis of dozens of instances.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic is getting more AI from less compute. That's great for Anthropic and bad for everyone else.
articles.title_zh: Anthropic is getting more AI from less compute. That's great for Anthropic and bad for everyone else.
articles.content_orig:
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
I have added shares of Anthropic ( NASDAQ:ANT ) in every session since it started trading, and each dip draws my attention back to the business. The stock closed at $87.64 on November 23, down 9.81% from the $97.17 level of November 19. To me, that pullback lowers the valuation of a leading AI consumption engine. This position sits in the growth part of my long-term portfolio, where I want decades of compounding.
Seat-based software grows when a customer hires another person. Anthropic grows when Claude does more work. Every agent run, coding session and API call adds to the meter. Consumption-based revenue rose from $288 million, or 75% of total revenue, in 2024 to $3.8 billion, or 83%, in 2025. In the first half of 2026 it reached $13.1 billion, or 80%. Management expects consumption to remain “the substantial majority of total revenue for the foreseeable future.”
First, scale. On its November 17 [ 1 ] earnings call, NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) said Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached $81 billion at the end of October. That run rate compares with a market value of roughly $677.5 billion.
Second, cheaper tokens drive more usage. Token prices fell nearly 60% since May [ 1 ] , yet weekly token volume on OpenRouter grew 35x year over year. Agentic workloads now make up about 80% of tokens [ 1 ] . Agents run longer and consume more. A seat license tops out at headcount, while a meter keeps running as long as the work does.
Third, access to compute. NVIDIA “expanded Anthropic’s access to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers” and keeps tuning future chips for Anthropic’s workloads. Anthropic’s S-1 describes a loop where enterprise revenue “helps us to fund the compute, research, and talent needed to improve Claude.”
The obvious alternative is NVIDIA, which reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.84 billion [ 2 ] , up 103.21% from a year earlier. That growth is significant. Its balance sheet also carries $390 billion [ 2 ] in supply commitments and guarantee exposure of up to $118 billion. It guided fourth-quarter gross margin down to 71.0% to 72.0% [ 2 ] during the Rubin ramp. Leadership turmoil added volatility. The company reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after his resignation, and the stock jumped 31.48% in Monday’s session. NVIDIA expects frontier labs to supply about 15% of its data center revenue this year [ 1 ] . The labs creating that demand look like the better holding.
Anthropic’s own filing warns that recent growth may reflect “early-stage adoption dynamics” and that the growth rate will decline over time, possibly faster than management expects. Its compute commitments stretch out to 2045. If token prices fall faster than volume grows, those fixed costs will squeeze margins. I also have only three sessions of trading history to judge the stock.
Demand still keeps outpacing supply. NVIDIA says its compute remains “fully utilized across every hyperscaler and neocloud we serve,” [ 1 ] and cloud industry backlog reached $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months earlier. Falling prices have so far pulled in more usage.
Anthropic released Claude 5.5 [ 1 ] , and each stronger model takes on more tasks for customers. More tasks mean more tokens, and more tokens mean more revenue. While the world keeps feeding work into Claude, that meter keeps running. That search for the lab, or the chip company, or the infrastructure name that compounds for a decade is the exercise we walked through in a free playbook on spotting the next monster tech winner early: here .

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, according to the Coast Guard.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage of the aircraft after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore, according to officials. There were four adults and two boys on board, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
The Jackson County Coroner's Office identified the passengers as Brent Stokes, 50, Michael Knox, 43, Arlyn Knox, 43, Hunter Stokes, 16, Charles Holden Knox, 12 and Truett Knox, 10. The Coast Guard previously said the young boys were 10 and 8 years old.
Everyone on board was related and from Fort Myers, Florida, where they were headed, the coroner's office said. The Cessna had departed from New Orleans, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama reported at about 3:45 p.m. that it had lost contact with the aircraft, the Coast Guard said.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when contact was lost, CBS Biloxi, Miss. affiliate WLOX-TV reported , citing the Coast Guard.
Responders spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.
Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard Sector Mobile Search and Rescue Mission Coordinator, called the situation heartbreaking.
"While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families," he said in a statement.
The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, with the NTSB taking the lead.
Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

articles.title_orig: Court casts heavy doubt over most serious Netanyahu charges, in huge blow to prosecution
articles.title_zh: Court casts heavy doubt over most serious Netanyahu charges, in huge blow to prosecution
articles.content_orig:
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

articles.title_orig: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say
articles.title_zh: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.title_orig: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.title_zh: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.content_orig:
London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.
The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.
Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.
Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.
"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."
One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."
Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."
Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.
"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.

articles.title_zh: China's Hansoh Pharma strikes drug deal with Bayer unit worth nearly $3.3 billion
articles.content_orig:
China Southern Airlines said in a filing late Tuesday that its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines had agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of approximately $7.4 billion.
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he expected China to purchase another 250 Boeing aircraft, following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit last week.
"By the way, I sold 250 Boeings to China, and I think they're going to do another 250," Trump said.
In May, China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines following Trump's visit to Beijing, marking the country's first commitment to purchase U.S.-made Boeing aircraft since 2017, according to the White House.
It was not immediately clear whether Xiamen Airlines' latest purchase was part of that commitment.
China Southern, which owns a 55% stake in Xiamen Airlines, said the actual purchase price would be lower than the combined list price because of discounts offered by Boeing. The company did not disclose the final purchase price, citing confidentiality provisions in the agreement.
The aircraft are scheduled to be delivered in batches between 2031 and 2034, with the purchase financed through a combination of internal funds and external financing, the filing showed. The transaction remains subject to shareholder and relevant Chinese government approvals.
China Southern said the purchase would support Xiamen Airlines' planned relocation to the new Xiamen Xiang'an International Airport and the expansion of its route network.
The agreement follows the group's recent purchase agreement for 137 Airbus A320neo - family aircraft, the filing showed. China Southern said sourcing aircraft from different manufacturers would help diversify its fleet and improve operational flexibility.
Other Asian carriers, including Philippine Airlines and Malaysia Aviation Group , have also announced Boeing aircraft orders this month.

articles.title_orig: Bond market fears a Jensen flop more than Warsh going soft
articles.title_zh: Bond market fears a Jensen flop more than Warsh going soft
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia, AMD, and Micron stocks sink as investors flee AI trade
articles.title_zh: Nvidia, AMD, and Micron stocks sink as investors flee AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock retreated another 8% on Wednesday, following a 6% decline in the prior session as chip stocks continued to plunge amid a broader market sell-off.
Peers AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) also extended losses from the prior session.
This year's once-hot AI trades continue to tumble, with memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) and peer SK Hynix ( SKHY ) tanking 11% and 8% respectively. Micron is more than 50% off its all-time high over the summer.
Storage and memory players Seagate (STX ), Western Digital ( WDC ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) all fell on Wednesday. Sandisk, which recently implemented a stock split, is down roughly 70% from its June record high.
The violent move follows a stunning rally on Monday when Nvidia jumped 31% after the AI chip giant's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. But some strategists say tighter financial conditions and lingering questions around the AI trade are weighing on sentiment.
"There is still a lot of nervousness out there, and some investors have taken advantage of Monday's jump to cut their exposure to the AI trade," said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, on Wednesday.
He also noted the prevailing view that Huang is the only person who can hold the AI trade together "reeks of desperation," while investors increasingly perceive that "Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want."
Other areas of the AI trade retreated on Wednesday, including the stocks of neocloud providers CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ), which each dropped by double-digit percentages.

articles.title_orig: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.title_zh: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.
The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
